title: "From pings to trips"
format: html

A trip (voyage) is the part of a vessel track between leaving port and
returning to port. In ramb, getting from raw pings to trips is the
entry of the fishing-activity flow: flag the pings (step 0), then cut
the track into voyages and put the trip back on each ping (step 1) —
see the [flow article](flow.html) for the full picture.

We use the `dansk` example data (Danish VMS
pings from
[WKSSFGEO](https://github.com/ices-eg/WKSSFGEO)) and the
`dansk_harbours` polygons, both shipped with the package as parquet and
read with [rb_read_example()](../reference/rb_read_example.html). First, rename to the grammar column names so
every function runs on its defaults — alternatively, pass e.g.
`vid = vessel_id, time = time_stamp` to each call.

```{r}
library(ramb)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

d <-
  rb_read_example("dansk") |>
  collect() |>
  arrange(vessel_id, time_stamp) |>
  rename(vid = vessel_id, time = time_stamp)
```

## Step 0: flag the pings

Flagging sets a `ping_flag` column; no row is ever dropped. A position
that is a placeholder rather than a fix is `"invalid"`
([rb_flag_ping_invalid()](../reference/rb_flag_ping_invalid.html)):

```{r}
d <- d |> rb_flag_ping_invalid()
```

A position the vessel cannot have reached — implied speed above
`kn_max` knots — is flagged by [rb_flag_ping_impossible()](../reference/rb_flag_ping_impossible.html). Its five
`method`s differ in how much of the surrounding track they consult;
`"clean"` is the fast default:

```{r}
d <- d |> rb_flag_ping_impossible(method = "clean")
d |> count(ping_flag)
```

The label names the filter stage that raised the flag — `"vmask"` from
the speed-distance-angle screen (the algorithm of
[argosfilter::sdafilter()](https://cran.r-project.org/package=argosfilter),
[Freitas et al. 2008](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1748-7692.2007.00180.x)),
`"forward"` from the forward scan against the last retained ping.

A third flagger, [rb_flag_ping_duplicate()](../reference/rb_flag_ping_duplicate.html), marks the lower-priority
feed's copy when several feeds report the same fix.

Finally, tag each ping with the port polygon it lies in
([rb_flag_ping_port()](../reference/rb_flag_ping_port.html)). `port_id` is a value in port, `NA` at sea —
this is the column trips are cut on. The flagged pings are set aside
(kept in `flagged` for the maps below); nothing is deleted:

```{r}
# the polygons as sf, from the WKB that DuckDB's geometry collects to
harbours <- rb_read_example("dansk_harbours") |> collect()
harbours <- sf::st_sf(
  port_id = harbours$SI_HARB,
  geometry = sf::st_as_sfc(structure(harbours$geometry, class = "WKB"), crs = 4326)
)

flagged <- d |> filter(!is.na(ping_flag))

d <-
  d |>
  filter(is.na(ping_flag)) |>
  rb_flag_ping_port(harbours)
```

## Step 1: cut the track into voyages

[rb_cut_trip_voyages()](../reference/rb_cut_trip_voyages.html) offers four rules (`method`); here we compare
two of them:

* `method = "runs"`: every run of pings in port, however short, ends a
  voyage.
* `method = "jepol"`: the ICES VMS datacall rule (`define_trips_pol`,
  after [vmstools](https://github.com/nielshintzen/vmstools),
  [Hintzen et al. 2012](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.fishres.2011.11.007)).
  A voyage runs from the first ping at sea to the first ping back in
  port; voyages shorter than `min_dur_h` hours are dropped, and voyages
  longer than `max_dur_h` hours are split at long gaps between pings.

```{r}
jepol <- rb_cut_trip_voyages(d, method = "jepol")
runs  <- rb_cut_trip_voyages(d, method = "runs")
```

Both return one row per voyage: vessel, year, voyage id, start and end
time, the ports departed from and returned to, and the number of pings.

```{r}
jepol
```

The two rules largely agree on these data; the jepol rule drops a few
short harbour-to-harbour runs:

```{r}
count(jepol, vid, name = "voyages_jepol") |>
  full_join(count(runs, vid, name = "voyages_runs"), by = "vid")
```

A third rule, `method = "stays"`, cuts the track at port *stays* found
by [rb_find_trip_stays()](../reference/rb_find_trip_stays.html) — stays being longer stops, so brief harbour
passages do not end a voyage. That is the rule used in the full
fishing-activity flow.

## Putting the trip back on the pings

[rb_assign_trip()](../reference/rb_assign_trip.html) joins the voyage table back onto the pings. Each
ping gets a `trip_id` and a `trip_basis` — `"reconstructed"` when the
trip was rebuilt from the track, `"none"` where no voyage covers the
ping (the port pings here):

```{r}
p <- d |> rb_assign_trip(jepol)
p |> count(trip_basis)
```

## The cut, in maps

Toggle the layers (top right of each map) to look at one trip at a
time. The maps are [mapview](https://r-spatial.github.io/mapview/)
leaflets.

### Two clean trips

`EX_3`, September 2020 — two voyages out of port 917, no flagged pings
anywhere in their windows:

* **Voyage 3** (Sep 15, ~8 h at sea): a simple out-and-back day trip,
  south along the coast and home again.
* **Voyage 4** (Sep 17–18, ~12 h): an overnight trip — out in the
  evening, fishing through the night, back before dawn.

```{r}
library(mapview)

as_line <- function(x) {
  x |>
    arrange(time) |>
    sf::st_as_sf(coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326) |>
    sf::st_combine() |>
    sf::st_cast("LINESTRING") |>
    sf::st_sf()
}

ex3 <- p |> filter(vid == "EX_3", lubridate::year(time) == 2020, voyage_id %in% 3:4)

mapview(harbours |> filter(port_id == 917),
        col.regions = "orange", alpha.regions = 0.4, layer.name = "Port 917") +
  mapview(ex3 |> filter(voyage_id == 3) |> as_line(),
          color = "steelblue", lwd = 2, layer.name = "Voyage 3 (Sep 15)") +
  mapview(ex3 |> filter(voyage_id == 4) |> as_line(),
          color = "darkred", lwd = 2, layer.name = "Voyage 4 (Sep 17-18)")
```

On clean tracks like these the choice of cutting rule is immaterial:
each run at sea is one voyage under both `"runs"` and `"jepol"`, and
the two tables row-match exactly. The rules only earn their keep when
the track is less tidy — as next.

### When the rules disagree

`EX_10`, July 2014, out of port 141. The runs rule cuts seven voyages
this year, the jepol rule five — the difference is one afternoon:

* **The day's trip** (blue): out at 04:08, back at 11:25. Both rules
  agree on it.
* **Two mini-voyages** (red): brief out-and-backs the same afternoon,
  at 14:37 and 14:53, each under ten minutes. `"runs"` takes every port
  departure literally and makes them voyages 5 and 6; `"jepol"` drops
  any voyage shorter than `min_dur_h` (0.5 h), so these pings end up
  with `trip_basis = "none"`.
* **One flagged ping** (black): a `"forward"` flag from step 0, set
  aside before cutting, so it takes no part in either rule.

```{r}
ex10 <-
  d |>
  rb_assign_trip(runs) |>
  filter(vid == "EX_10", lubridate::date(time) == as.Date("2014-07-18"))

mapview(harbours |> filter(port_id == 141),
        col.regions = "orange", alpha.regions = 0.4, layer.name = "Port 141") +
  mapview(ex10 |> filter(voyage_id == 4) |> as_line(),
          color = "steelblue", lwd = 2, layer.name = "Day trip (04:08-11:25)") +
  mapview(ex10 |> filter(voyage_id %in% 5:6) |>
            sf::st_as_sf(coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326),
          col.regions = "red", cex = 4, layer.name = "Mini-voyages (runs only)") +
  mapview(flagged |> filter(vid == "EX_10", lubridate::date(time) == as.Date("2014-07-18")) |>
            sf::st_as_sf(coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326),
          col.regions = "black", cex = 6, layer.name = "Flagged ping")
```

Which is right? If the afternoon runs were the skipper moving berth or
testing the engine, dropping them (jepol) is honest; if gear was in the
water, only `"runs"` keeps them. The third rule, `"stays"`, goes the
other way entirely: it ends a voyage only at a *stay*, so a brief
harbour passage mid-trip would not split the day's trip either.

### Trouble pings that bend the track

`EX_10` again, a year earlier — the morning of Oct 6, 2013, mid-way
through a three-day voyage out of port 141. Here the badness needs no
diagnostics:

* **The raw track** (grey): sixteen impossible positions drag the line
  up to 33 km off the grounds and back within minutes — while the
  vessel's own speed sensor reads ~6 knots throughout.
* **The clean track** (blue): the same morning after step 0; the
  voyage's shape is unchanged, the spikes are gone.
* **The flagged pings** (red): `"vmask"` and `"forward"` flags. This is
  the failure mode the speed filters are built for, and every `method`
  catches these.

```{r}
t1 <- as.POSIXct("2013-10-06 05:00", tz = "UTC")
t2 <- as.POSIXct("2013-10-06 13:30", tz = "UTC")
clean6 <- d |> filter(vid == "EX_10", time >= t1, time <= t2)
flag6  <- flagged |> filter(vid == "EX_10", time >= t1, time <= t2)

mapview(harbours |> filter(port_id == 141),
        col.regions = "orange", alpha.regions = 0.4, layer.name = "Port 141") +
  mapview(bind_rows(clean6, flag6) |> as_line(),
          color = "grey40", lwd = 2, layer.name = "Raw track (flags kept)") +
  mapview(clean6 |> as_line(),
          color = "steelblue", lwd = 2, layer.name = "Clean track (flags set aside)") +
  mapview(flag6 |> sf::st_as_sf(coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326),
          col.regions = "red", cex = 6, layer.name = "Flagged pings")
```

The same morning as the speed filter sees it — implied speed of each
ping against its predecessor (with [rb_calc_distance()](../reference/rb_calc_distance.html)), log scale.
Every spike is orders of magnitude above the 25-knot ceiling (dashed),
while the honest track never exceeds ~10 kn:

```{r}
diag6 <-
  bind_rows(clean6, flag6) |>
  arrange(time) |>
  mutate(dt = as.numeric(difftime(time, lag(time), units = "secs")),
         kn = rb_calc_distance(lag(lon), lag(lat), lon, lat) / dt * 1.94384,
         flag = ifelse(is.na(ping_flag), "kept", ping_flag))

ggplot(diag6 |> filter(!is.na(kn)), aes(time, kn, colour = flag)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.8) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 25, linetype = 2, colour = "grey40") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(kept = "grey70", forward = "red",
                                 vmask = "orange")) +
  labs(y = "Implied speed [kn, log scale]", colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

The few *kept* points above the line are the returns-to-track right
after a spike: the filter's anchor is the last *retained* ping, so the
comeback is measured against the last good position and passes.

Because the flags are set aside first, neither cutting rule is confused
by the spikes: the voyage is cut on the clean pings, and the voyage
window then covers the gaps. This is why step 0 flags rather than drops
— the flagged pings still exist for audit, but they cannot bend the
trip boundaries.

### Side point: when the flagged pings sit *on* the track

Not every flag is a spike. Back to Jul 19, 2014 on the same vessel:
eight flags inside the voyage window, yet on a map most of them sit on
the track. The diagnostic that separates the cases is implied speed
against time — each ping measured against its predecessor:

```{r}
raw5 <-
  p |>
  filter(vid == "EX_10", voyage_id == 5, lubridate::year(time) == 2014) |>
  bind_rows(flagged |>
              filter(vid == "EX_10",
                     lubridate::date(time) == as.Date("2014-07-19"))) |>
  arrange(time) |>
  mutate(dt = as.numeric(difftime(time, lag(time), units = "secs")),
         kn = rb_calc_distance(lag(lon), lag(lat), lon, lat) / dt * 1.94384,
         flag = ifelse(is.na(ping_flag), "kept", ping_flag))

ggplot(raw5 |> filter(!is.na(kn)), aes(time, kn, colour = flag)) +
  geom_point(size = 1.2) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 25, linetype = 2, colour = "grey50") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(kept = "grey70", forward = "red",
                                 vmask = "orange")) +
  labs(y = "Implied speed [kn, log scale]", colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

Two regimes, one morning apart: a lone point at 264 kn — the same kind
of spike as above, correctly flagged — and a cluster straddling the
25-knot threshold in the last hour before landing. The turn-angle view
adds a clue: a working vessel turns constantly, but the flagged cluster
sits at ~175 degrees — positions jumping almost straight back, the
fingerprint of a track alternating between two sources:

```{r}
raw5 |>
  mutate(brg = atan2(lon - lag(lon), lat - lag(lat)) * 180 / pi,
         turn = (brg - lag(brg) + 540) %% 360 - 180) |>
  filter(!is.na(turn)) |>
  ggplot(aes(time, abs(turn), colour = flag)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(kept = "grey70", forward = "red",
                                 vmask = "orange")) +
  labs(y = "|Turn| [deg]", colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

Zooming into that last hour reveals not glitches but **two interleaved
emission streams**:

* a dense, self-consistent stream — a ping every ~10 s, ~36 m steps,
  ~7 kn, matching the vessel's speed sensor exactly;
* a sparse stream (~every 60 s, always at `:39`/`:40` seconds) whose
  positions zigzag against the dense track — the signature of a second,
  lower-quality feed (or a delayed secondary channel) reporting the
  same voyage.

The forward filter anchors on the last *retained* ping, so a retained
sparse ping poisons the next measurement: the innocent dense ping after
it shows 175 m in 11 s = 31 kn and gets flagged. Of the seven
`"forward"` flags that afternoon, five are innocent dense pings —
collateral damage — while most of the sparse stream survives every
method. This is precisely what [rb_flag_ping_duplicate()](../reference/rb_flag_ping_duplicate.html) exists for,
and because flagged pings are never used as anchors by later flaggers,
running it first repairs the anchors:

```{r}
raw5 |>
  select(vid, time, lon, lat) |>
  mutate(feed = if_else(lubridate::second(time) %in% c(39, 40),
                        "sparse", "dense")) |>
  rb_flag_ping_duplicate(priority = c("dense", "sparse"),
                         feed = feed, max_dt_s = 15) |>
  rb_flag_ping_impossible(method = "clean") |>
  count(ping_flag)
```

Every sparse ping is flagged `"duplicate"`, the true spike is still
caught — and not a single dense ping is flagged. Two honest caveats:
the `feed` labels here are inferred from the emission cadence (`dansk`
has no provider column; real data would), and this two-stream
fingerprint is not everywhere — across `dansk` it is confined to
`EX_10` and `EX_11`, but there it accounts for most of their flags,
while the other vessels' flags are sparse true spikes. Inferring these
streams without a feed column is open work; for now, know your feeds
and flag duplicates before impossibles.

From here the flow continues with the logbook record (step 2): which
declared trip or haul covers each ping. [rb_link_trip_logbook()](../reference/rb_link_trip_logbook.html) builds
the VMS-to-logbook crosswalk for that.
